summary: Vietnam veteran Robert K. Brown founded Soldier of Fortune magazine in 1975, using it to recruit Americans for white-ruled Rhodesia, run classified ads that led to contract murders, and feed the US militia movement.

evidence.note: Brown's birth in 1932 in Monroe, Michigan opens the biography
Oman mercenary-contract scheme money funds the new magazine in 1975
long Rhodesia segment begins: the white-minority state and its war
magazine recruiting articles drew about 400 Americans into the Rhodesian army
recruit via classified ad captured and executed in Angola in 1976
Savage places a gun-for-hire ad and carries out contract killings
trucker Hearn's ad brings murder offers; he kills Sandra Black
hitman ads stop in 1986; civil judgment upheld on appeal
Brown joins mercenaries backing D'Aubuisson in El Salvador from 1983
magazine boosts militias; McVeigh subscriber, zine traced to its office (1995)
post-1990s pivot to border vigilantes (2003) and Arpaio (2009)
magazine goes online-only; 2019 republication shows ongoing legacy

notes: Live show at Dynasty Typewriter. Brown treated as co-primary with the magazine since his biography frames the story, so the lifetime rule sets covered_span 1932-2020; lifespan end null because he was alive at release (verify current status). No theme for murder-for-hire or mercenary recruiting; immigration (Ranch Rescue, Arpaio) and the arms trade are brief and left out.
